n5-aka.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Earth</radical> baked until it gives up all its water turns the only colour it can, which is <kanji>red</kanji>.
n5-aka.reading_mnemonic: The guy who lit that underground fire is Seki, and he's coughing his lungs out from the smoke — a wet, rattling <reading>せき</reading> that won't stop as long as the red embers keep burning. Every time he sees red he starts up again: せき, せき, せき.
n5-aka.description: Means "red"; a common color kanji that shows up in words for the color itself and things like traffic lights.

n5-ame-rain.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the window and watch <radical>rain</radical> streak down the glass, drop by drop. Each drop lands inside its own tiny square of the frame. Rows of falling drops trapped in a frame are what we call <kanji>rain</kanji>.
n5-ame-rain.reading_mnemonic: A cow gets caught outside in the downpour and lets out a long, miserable "<reading>う</reading>ー" as the drops soak her. Every time it rains, that cow's soggy うー is the sound you hear.
n5-ame-rain.description: Means "rain"; the base kanji for weather words and it sits on top of many other weather-related characters as a component.

n5-ao.meaning_mnemonic: A tiny sprout curls up over the <radical>moon</radical> one clear night. Moonlight turns its leaves an odd <radical>blue-green</radical>, somewhere between sky and grass. That strange in-between color is what everyone calls <kanji>blue</kanji>.
n5-ao.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, holds up a jar of blue-green ink and says the color is called 「<reading>せい</reading>」 — of course she knew it first. She's already dipping her perfect brush in before anyone else can answer.
n5-ao.description: Means blue or green (the fresh blue-green range); shows up in color words and in compounds about youth and freshness.

n5-ashi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> sits on top of a pair of legs. The legs have skidded to a halt — they are <radical>stopping</radical> hard. They end in one part: a <radical>foot</radical>. That's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg, plenty to stand on.
n5-ashi.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「<reading>そく</reading>、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
n5-ashi.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

n5-atarashii.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>axe</radical> taken to a <radical>tree</radical> that used to <radical>stand</radical> there leaves you timber that is completely <kanji>new</kanji>.
n5-atarashii.reading_mnemonic: The showroom greeter is Shin, and every time a new model rolls in he shouts his own name — <reading>しん</reading>! — as he yanks the cover off. Whatever Shin unveils is always brand new.
n5-atarashii.description: Means "new"; a very common kanji appearing in words for new things, newspapers, and freshness.

n5-bun-minute.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter prises a chipped <radical>sword</radical> out of its frozen rice cake and wipes it clean. She gives it one job: split a log. It comes down clean, and the two halves lean apart into a fresh <radical>eight</radical>. One <kanji>minute</kanji>, one cut, and the sword finally earns its keep.
n5-bun-minute.reading_mnemonic: The woodcutter, sawdust in her eyebrows, times herself at one log a minute and calls it the most <reading>fun</reading> you can have before breakfast. The sword, back in her hands and still chipped, snorts <reading>ふん</reading> — it was the one doing all the work.

n5-chikara.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>power</radical> radical and the <kanji>power</kanji> kanji are the same character, and strength is just that same power once you can feel it straining in your muscles.
n5-chikara.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a weightlifter decides the vending machine at the top is a better workout than the climb. She wraps both arms around it, heaves it up, and roars <reading>りょく</reading> as if the mountain had tried to <reading>rock</reading> her loose. It still drops one cold can when she sets it down.
n5-chikara.description: The one to watch is 九, 'nine'. In 力 the long stroke drops straight down the right side and ends in a small hook curling to the left. In 九 that stroke swings out wide to the right and finishes with a hook low on the right, and its first stroke pokes out past the top-left corner.

n5-dai-big.meaning_mnemonic: Here is one that costs you nothing, since the <radical>big</radical> radical, arms and legs flung wide, is already the finished <kanji>big</kanji> kanji.
n5-dai-big.reading_mnemonic: Dai, the giant baby, is truck-sized, and his crying registers as real earthquakes. When the mountain-trail vending machine takes his coin and drops nothing, he lets out one <reading>だい</reading> bellow you feel in your chest three switchbacks down. Hikers now call any tremor on that path a <reading>Dai</reading>.
n5-dai-big.description: The look-alikes are 太 (thick), 天 (heaven), and 犬 (dog). All four are the same wide-armed figure with splayed legs. 大 has nothing added. 太 adds one short dot low between the legs. 天 lays a long flat stroke across the very top, above the arms. That top stroke is longer than the arm stroke. 犬 adds one small dot high on the right, near the arm. Any extra mark means it is not 大.

n5-denki-den.meaning_mnemonic: A flash brighter than the <radical>sun</radical> tearing straight down through the <radical>rain</radical> is raw <kanji>electricity</kanji>.
n5-denki-den.reading_mnemonic: The lightning hits a power line and the whole street goes DEN — <reading>でん</reading> — every fluorescent tube in Koichi's konbini surging bright at once. You feel that でん in your teeth as the electricity floods back.
n5-denki-den.description: Means "electricity"; shows up in everyday words for trains, phones, lights, and anything electrical.

n5-deru.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you see one <radical>mountain</radical> stacked right on top of another mountain — two sets of three peaks piled up. When the peaks get that tall, there's only one thing you want to do: get out and leave. So this doubled-up mountain means <kanji>exit</kanji>, leave.
n5-deru.reading_mnemonic: At the exit of the mountain trail stands a hiker who sneezes so hard every time someone leaves — a huge "<reading>しゅつ</reading>!" — that the whole vending machine rattles. Every time you head for the exit, you hear that "しゅつ" behind you.
n5-deru.description: Means exit or leave; shows up in everyday words about going out, leaving, and departures.

n5-do-earth.meaning_mnemonic: You met this shape already as the <radical>earth</radical> radical, and the <kanji>earth</kanji> kanji is the very same character, used just as happily for the loose soil that earth breaks down into.
n5-do-earth.reading_mnemonic: A gardener lugs a sack of soil over to mark out her new patch of earth, loses her grip near the fence, and it drops with a deep <reading>ど</reading>. The sack splits like a giant ball of <reading>dough</reading> and buries her boots in soil.

n5-dokusho.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has to <radical>sell</radical> you the <radical>words</radical> before you can sit down anywhere and <kanji>read</kanji> them.
n5-dokusho.reading_mnemonic: The reader you find hunched over those lines of speech is a poison-pen critic, and you nickname her Doku (<reading>どく</reading>) because every review she reads she then tears apart. Watch her read a page and you can practically see the どく venom drip off her pen.

n5-eki-station.meaning_mnemonic: A galloping <radical>horse</radical> comes charging onto the platform out of nowhere. It leaps clean over a sleeping <radical>body</radical> lying across a bench. Commuters barely look up, just another morning at the <kanji>station</kanji>.
n5-eki-station.reading_mnemonic: A commuter named Eki misses the last train and shouts "<reading>えき</reading>! えき!" across the empty platform, hoping the station master will hear her and hold the doors.
n5-eki-station.description: Means "station" — the word for a train or subway station, seen constantly in place names and on transit signs.

n5-en.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> pinned at one end to the <radical>ground</radical> and swung all the way around the inside of a <radical>wide box</radical> scratches out the round coin you spend as one <kanji>yen</kanji>.
n5-en.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a young monk called <reading>Zen</reading> keeps trying to paint one flawless circle in a single brushstroke. Every time a shrine cat pads across the wet paper he mutters <reading>えん</reading> and reaches for a clean sheet, and by dusk the mossy steps are tiled with lopsided rings.

n5-furui.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> counts slowly to <radical>ten</radical> every single morning. It has counted so many mornings that the counting itself feels ancient. Something repeated this many times can only be <kanji>old</kanji>.
n5-furui.reading_mnemonic: Koichi finds an ancient rice ball at the very back of his konbini shelf, so far past its date the wrapper has yellowed. He picks it up, sighs, and mutters just one syllable at how old it is: 「<reading>こ</reading>」.
n5-furui.description: Means "old," as in old and worn from age; appears in words about age and antiquity and in the common word for "used/secondhand."

n5-gaku.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>small</radical> <radical>child</radical> under a <radical>cover</radical> with nothing to do but turn pages is going to <kanji>study</kanji>.
n5-gaku.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the star pupil Gaku is the one who never stops studying, and everyone in the echoing hallways calls out <reading>がく</reading> whenever they need the answer. Hear がく and you hear the kid who lives to learn.
n5-gaku.description: Means study or learning; a very common kanji that shows up in words for student, school, and academic subjects.

n5-gatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> radical and the <kanji>month</kanji> kanji are the same character, which makes sense once you remember a month is just one lap of the moon.
n5-gatsu.reading_mnemonic: Once a month the night janitor at Sei's school, a man called <reading>Getz</reading>, mops the echoing hallway by the light of the full moon. The moonlight through the tall windows lights up every streak he missed, so he groans <reading>げつ</reading> and mops the whole floor over again.

n5-go-language.meaning_mnemonic: A waterfall of <radical>speech</radical> pours down into a waiting <radical>mouth</radical> below. The mouth swallows every word whole without chewing once. Stuffed with so many words, it finally speaks a whole <kanji>language</kanji>.
n5-go-language.reading_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini, a chatty regular named Go won't stop talking. Every single language pours out of him at once, and the only word you catch is his own name: <reading>ご</reading>, ご, ご.

n5-go.meaning_mnemonic: You already met <radical>five</radical> as a radical, and the <kanji>five</kanji> kanji is that same shape with nothing added.
n5-go.reading_mnemonic: Five runners crouch in the blocks on Sei's school sports field. The starter means to shout the English word <reading>go</reading>, but it keeps coming out as <reading>ご</reading>. On the fifth flat little <reading>ご</reading>, all five of them finally sprint.

n5-hachi.meaning_mnemonic: There is no work to do on this one, since the radical <radical>eight</radical> and the <kanji>eight</kanji> kanji are one and the same character.
n5-hachi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi pulls a fresh <reading>batch</reading> of steamed buns from the warmer, eight of them, and lines them along the tray by the till. He taps each bun as he counts, and the tray tips when he reaches the eighth and says <reading>はち</reading>. Eight buns, and <reading>はち</reading> is the one that rolls onto the floor.
n5-hachi.description: The look-alikes are 入 (enter) and 人 (person). In 人 the two strokes join in a sharp peak at the top. In 入 they meet near the top too, but the right stroke pokes up past the join. In 八 the strokes never touch, leaving an open gap at the top.

n5-hairu.meaning_mnemonic: Watch the shape closely: it's a little figure ducking their head as they <radical>enter</radical> through a low doorway. You lean, you dip, you step through — and just like that, you <kanji>enter</kanji>.
n5-hairu.reading_mnemonic: The figure ducking through the door is a new student, and as they enter the echoing school hallway everyone whispers "the new one, <reading>にゅう</reading>, the new one." Every time someone new enters, that にゅう ripples down the hall.
n5-hairu.description: 入, 人 and 八 are the same pair of strokes. In 入 the short left stroke begins partway down the long one, leaving a small overhang at the top. 人 meets at a clean point, and 八 never lets the two touch.

n5-hana.meaning_mnemonic: When ordinary <radical>grass</radical> gets tired of being green and <radical>change</radical>s its top into colour, what stands there is a <kanji>flower</kanji>.
n5-hana.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow lands on the wire above your flowerbed and lets out a scratchy <reading>caw</reading>. A puff of flame slips out with the sound and singes the newest bloom black. He looks down at his work and croaks <reading>か</reading>, thoroughly pleased with himself.

n5-hanashi-wa.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of <radical>speech</radical> leans in close, and right beside it a <radical>tongue</radical> sticks out of a mouth, wagging nonstop. Put the speech next to the busy tongue and you've got someone who just won't stop talking, spinning story after <kanji>story</kanji>.
n5-hanashi-wa.reading_mnemonic: Wanda the storyteller loves an audience, so she waves both hands and calls out "<reading>わ</reading>!" every time she starts a new tale. That little "わ" is her signal that another long talk is about to begin.
n5-hanashi-wa.description: Means talk or story; shows up in everyday words for speaking, conversation, and telephone.

n5-hantime.meaning_mnemonic: A shape with a pair of <radical>horns</radical> above a <radical>cross</radical>, sliced straight down to the <radical>ground</radical>, leaves each side holding exactly one <kanji>half</kanji>.
n5-hantime.reading_mnemonic: Behind the counter at Koichi's konbini, <reading>Han</reading> the half-and-half chef lifts every onigiri off the shelf and slices it clean down the middle before he will ring it up. Ask him why, and he just holds up the two matching pieces and says his own name, <reading>はん</reading>.
n5-hantime.description: Keep this apart from 羊, sheep, which lines up three horizontal bars beneath its horns and lets its centre stroke stop at the lowest bar. Half has only two bars, and its centre stroke drives straight through the bottom one and pokes out underneath.

n5-hayai.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is barely <radical>ten</radical> fingers above the horizon, which means you are up <kanji>early</kanji>.
n5-hayai.reading_mnemonic: There's a rooster at Grandma Kane's shrine who crows the moment the sun peeks over the mossy steps, way too early: "<reading>そう</reading>! そう!" he screams, so loud the cats scatter. Now you're up before dawn whether you like it or not.
n5-hayai.description: Means "early" or "fast," and shows up in everyday words about time and speed like 早い (early/fast) and 早く (quickly).

n5-hidari.meaning_mnemonic: Your flat <radical>left hand</radical> exists to hold the <radical>construction</radical> girder still while your other hand does the bolting, so <kanji>left</kanji> just means the bracing hand.
n5-hidari.reading_mnemonic: Sara steadies the construction beam with her left hand, exactly as that hand is built to do, and drives the saw with her right. Every stroke drags a dry <reading>さ</reading> out of the plank, the flat sound of a <reading>saw</reading> in soft pine. She keeps going until the whole site is ankle deep in sawdust.
n5-hidari.description: The look-alike is 右, meaning right. Both share the flat left-hand stroke across the top; the giveaway sits underneath, where left carries the construction beam and right holds a small closed box instead. In left the horizontal top stroke is the long one, while in right the slanting stroke is longer and the horizontal stays short.

n5-hidariuma.meaning_mnemonic: Held straight overhead at <kanji>noon</kanji>, a bone-<radical>dry</radical> shield throws almost no shadow, just one thin <radical>slash</radical>, because the sun is standing directly above it.
n5-hidariuma.reading_mnemonic: At the school sports field, a gopher called <reading>Gordon</reading> only surfaces at noon, when the sun sits straight overhead and not one shadow falls to warn him. The moment the lunch bell blares <reading>ご</reading>, he bolts across the bright grass for the echoing hallways.
n5-hidariuma.description: Two kanji crowd the same outline. 千, thousand, carries just one horizontal bar where noon stacks two, and it opens with a short flat tick instead of noon's longer left-falling slash. 牛, cow, is the nearer miss: its centre post pushes up through the top stroke, while noon's vertical stops flush against a slanted top and never breaks above it.

n5-higashi.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's <kanji>east</kanji>.
n5-higashi.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

n5-hito-jin.meaning_mnemonic: Knowing your radicals pays off here, because the <radical>person</radical> radical is the <kanji>person</kanji> kanji with nothing added and nothing changed.
n5-hito-jin.reading_mnemonic: Jin, the friendly giant, bends double to fit through the door of Koichi's konbini and clips the onigiri shelf every single time. As the rice balls roll across the floor he sighs <reading>じん</reading>, because a person the size of <reading>Jin</reading> spends his whole life apologising for doorways.
n5-hito-jin.description: The look-alikes are 入 (enter) and 八 (eight). In 人 the two strokes join in a sharp peak at the top with nothing poking out above the join. In 入 they meet near the top too, but the right stroke pushes up past the join like a small flag. In 八 the two strokes never touch, leaving an open gap at the top and spreading apart like a fan.

n5-hoku.meaning_mnemonic: A tortoise doing <radical>divination</radical> in the fading <radical>evening</radical> light has to shuffle <kanji>outside</kanji> to catch the last of the sun on its cracked shell.
n5-hoku.reading_mnemonic: Out behind Grandma Kane's shrine at dusk, a fortune-telling guy keeps flipping his tortoise shell for one more reading. Each blank answer drags a long <reading>がい</reading> out of him, the groan a worn-out <reading>guy</reading> makes when the cards say wait.

n5-hon.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing tall, with the <radical>ground</radical> drawn as one flat line across its trunk — right where the roots meet the soil. That line marks the tree's own origin. Press pages flat from that origin, and you have a <kanji>book</kanji>.
n5-hon.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>ほん</reading> sits on the mossy steps at Grandma Kane's shrine, reading the same book over and over. Every time a cat brushes past, he mutters "ほん, ほん" without looking up — he cannot put that book down.
n5-hon.description: 本 is 木 with one extra stroke: a short horizontal laid across the lower trunk. Nothing else changes, so that little bar down at the base is the only thing to look for.

n5-hyaku.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>one</radical> stroke sits on top of a blinding <radical>white</radical> light bulb. The light is so bright the stroke multiplies into copies of itself. Soon there are exactly a <kanji>hundred</kanji> strokes glowing on the ceiling.
n5-hyaku.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hiccuping cook keeps counting onigiri. Every time he hits a full tray, he lets out a huge "<reading>ひゃく</reading>!" — a hiccup and a yell in one. A hundred rice balls is a lot to hiccup through.
n5-hyaku.description: 百 is 白 with one extra stroke on top. 白 caps its box with a small flick; 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal bar.

n5-ichi.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ground</radical> radical is already in your head, and the <kanji>one</kanji> kanji is the very same flat line.
n5-ichi.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called <reading>Itchy</reading> drags himself up the mountain trail to the one vending machine at the top. Bitten raw by bugs, he claws at both arms and groans <reading>いち</reading> with every scratch. One machine, one word, one sound he cannot shake.

n5-iku-go.meaning_mnemonic: You already met the <radical>going</radical> radical, and the kanji for <kanji>go</kanji> is that same crossroads with not one stroke added, so take the free point.
n5-iku-go.reading_mnemonic: Koichi the konbini king cannot stand a customer who lingers, so the moment your bag is packed he slaps a <reading>coupon</reading> into your hand and barks <reading>こう</reading>, which in his shop means get going, right now. The regulars know the drill: hear <reading>こう</reading>, take the coupon, and go.

n5-iu-gen.meaning_mnemonic: Lines stacked above an open <radical>mouth</radical> are the sounds coming out of it the moment you <kanji>say</kanji> something.
n5-iu-gen.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a general in full armor climbs the mossy steps and won't stop giving orders — every word out of his mouth is a barked command. The cats scatter as the general says "<reading>げん</reading>!" like it's the only word he knows.

n5-jikan-ji.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> crossing the <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> roof is how the whole village used to tell the <kanji>time</kanji>.
n5-jikan-ji.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful clockmaker named Jiro keeps every timepiece in Koichi's konbini ticking, and each hour on the hour he shouts "<reading>じ</reading>! じ!" as the alarms go off. Whenever you need to know the time, you listen for Jiro's じ.
n5-jikan-ji.description: Means time or hour, and shows up everywhere you talk about clock time and telling the hour.

n5-juu.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ten</radical> radical and the <kanji>ten</kanji> kanji are the very same mark, so this is one you already know for free.
n5-juu.reading_mnemonic: You dump exactly ten cartons of <reading>juice</reading> onto the beeping till at Koichi's konbini. Just as he counts them off and lands on <reading>じゅう</reading> for the total, the bottom carton splits and sprays sticky juice clear across the onigiri shelf.
n5-juu.description: 十 is a single upright stroke crossed by one flat horizontal. 千 (thousand) adds a short slash slanting in above that cross. 七 (seven) has no upright at all: one stroke bends and hooks up to the right beneath a high, tilted bar.

n5-ka-fire.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>fire</radical> radical, and the <kanji>fire</kanji> kanji is that same upright log with sparks flicking off both sides.
n5-ka-fire.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line above Koichi's konbini and opens her beak for one <reading>caw</reading>. A puff of flame rolls out instead, and the onigiri shelf by the door goes up black and smoking. That crow's <reading>か</reading> now sticks to every fire you meet.

n5-kaeru.meaning_mnemonic: Putting down the <radical>knife</radical> and picking up the <radical>sweeper</radical> is what you do the hour you <kanji>return</kanji> home.
n5-kaeru.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, has been out riding the wind all day, and now she giggles as she slips back inside her old tree with a soft <reading>き</reading>. Watch her return home and you'll hear that き every time.
n5-kaeru.description: Means "return," as in going or coming back home; the core kanji in the verb 帰る, to return.

n5-kaku-write.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>brush</radical> moving all <radical>day</radical> with nothing to show for it but marks means somebody had to <kanji>write</kanji>.
n5-kaku-write.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands on your notebook and squints at your terrible handwriting, muttering "<reading>しょ</reading>, しょ" every time you smudge a letter. Each little puff of flame dries the ink so you can keep writing.
n5-kaku-write.description: Means "write"; shows up in words about writing, documents, and books, like 書く (to write).

n5-kane-gold-dup.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole <radical>village</radical> at dusk, huddled around one big cooking fire. Smoke climbs and stains every wall <radical>black</radical>. It settles over the paddies, the packed earth, the wooden houses. The sooty village standing over that fire has turned one single colour: <kanji>black</kanji>.
n5-kane-gold-dup.reading_mnemonic: The soot-covered villagers cough up thick black lungfuls, hacking <reading>こく</reading>, こく into the night air. Every cough is darker than the last — that's the sound of black.
n5-kane-gold-dup.description: Means "black"; the everyday word for the color (くろ) and a common on'yomi こく in compounds.

n5-kau.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want, so you reach for the cowrie <radical>shell</radical> that once worked as money. You lay that shell on the counter and slide it across. Handing over the shell-money is how you <kanji>buy</kanji>.
n5-kau.reading_mnemonic: The moment you buy your onigiri at Koichi's konbini, Kaa the fire-breathing crow swoops in and shrieks 「<reading>ばい</reading>」 as if saying "bye-bye" to your cash before you've even paid.
n5-kau.description: Means "buy," the verb 買う (to purchase); shows up constantly in shopping and everyday transactions.

n5-kawa.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>river</radical> radical and the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji are the same character, drawn as the same three flowing strokes every single time.
n5-kawa.reading_mnemonic: A courier crouches at the riverbank, certain the fastest way to <reading>send</reading> a parcel across is to float it. The current takes it the instant it touches the water and skims it away downstream, hissing <reading>せん</reading> over the shallows.

n5-ki-spirit.meaning_mnemonic: A field's <kanji>spirit</kanji> is the <radical>steam</radical> that lifts off the blades the morning after you <radical>mow</radical> them down to stubble.
n5-ki-spirit.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit climbs out of her old oak beside the field you just mowed. Warm steam curls off the stubble and tickles her until she cannot stop giggling, a thin <reading>き</reading> sound like a tiny <reading>key</reading> scraping in a lock. She rides the vapour up and vanishes into the cold.

n5-kiku-hear.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>ear</radical> pressed to the crack in the <radical>gate</radical> is there for one reason, which is to <kanji>hear</kanji>.
n5-kiku-hear.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, press their ears to the gate to hear you ask a question. They immediately start arguing about the answer. "<reading>ぶん</reading>!" they squeak in unison. Those two never agree on anything they overhear.
n5-kiku-hear.description: 聞 and 間 are the same gate frame with different things standing inside it. 聞 puts 耳, an ear, in the gateway. 間 frames the sun there instead. What the gate contains is the whole difference.

n5-kin.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gold</radical> radical and the <kanji>gold</kanji> kanji are the very same character, which also came to mean money because for centuries gold coins were exactly what people paid with.
n5-kin.reading_mnemonic: A tiny king no taller than a coin lives on the collection box at Grandma Kane's shrine and sorts the offerings into his crown. Drop one in and he stands up and announces <reading>king</reading> with a small bow. That bright <reading>きん</reading> is the sound of money landing.

n5-kita.meaning_mnemonic: Here is one that comes free, because the <radical>north</radical> radical and the <kanji>north</kanji> kanji are the very same character, learned once and counted twice.
n5-kita.reading_mnemonic: Down at the frozen riverbank, two skaters stand back to back and guard the same net. Every time the puck clangs off the post they both bark <reading>ほく</reading>, the flat grunt a rink announcer makes yelling <reading>hockey</reading> into a dead microphone.

n5-ko-child.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>child</kanji> kanji is a gift you already own, the <radical>child</radical> radical exactly as you learned it, without a single stroke changed.
n5-ko-child.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, a small child keeps running laps and shrieking. The teacher on duty crouches down and makes a long <reading>し</reading> sound, the <reading>shush</reading> you do with one finger on your lips. The child copies the finger, copies the sound, and finally walks.

n5-kon-now.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>now</radical> radical is the <kanji>now</kanji> kanji with nothing changed, so this one is a free point if you learned your radicals.
n5-kon-now.reading_mnemonic: A shrine cat nudges a loose roof tile off the eaves and it lands square on a dozing raccoon, which bolts upright yelping <reading>こん</reading> as the tile <reading>conk</reading>s the step beside it. No warning comes first and no echo after, just the one hit landing right <reading>こん</reading>, meaning it lands now, this instant.
n5-kon-now.description: The look-alike is 会, 'meet'. Both wear the same wide peaked lid on top. Beneath the lid, 今 keeps almost nothing: a short flat dash above one small hooked stroke. 会 fills that space with a full horizontal line and a small angled shape sitting under it. Crowded underneath means 会; nearly empty with only a tiny tail means 今.

n5-kou-school.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> in a yard where children <radical>mingle</radical> between two bells is standing in a <kanji>school</kanji>.
n5-kou-school.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, has set up a pop-up shop right inside the school gate, restocking onigiri between classes and muttering <reading>こう</reading>, こう as he lines up the shelves. The kids buy their lunch from him before the bell.

n5-kuchi.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a freebie, because the <radical>mouth</radical> radical you already know is the whole <kanji>mouth</kanji> kanji, with nothing added.
n5-kuchi.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, taste-tests every new product the second it lands on his shelf. When he tips the just-boiled <reading>cocoa</reading> straight back into his mouth, he yelps one long <reading>こう</reading> that rattles the onigiri shelf and sets the till beeping.

n5-kuni.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>jewel</radical> kept inside an <radical>enclosure</radical> that nobody may cross is what makes a <kanji>country</kanji>.
n5-kuni.reading_mnemonic: At the border of this walled country stands a guard named Koku, who stamps every passport with a cheerful <reading>こく</reading> sound. No stamp, no entry — こく, こく, all day long.
n5-kuni.description: Means "country" or "nation"; a very common kanji seen in words for countries and citizenship, read こく in compounds and くに on its own.

n5-kuru-rai.meaning_mnemonic: When a single grain of <radical>rice</radical> bursts apart and the pieces scatter over the flat <radical>ground</radical>, a whole crop is about to <kanji>come</kanji> up where each one landed.
n5-kuru-rai.reading_mnemonic: A heron that roosts in the rye grass by the riverbank bolts upright at every thunderclap, flaps into the same low branch with a thud, and squawks <reading>らい</reading>. Beak still stuck in the <reading>rye</reading>, it has decided <reading>らい</reading> is the noise you make when something unstoppable is about to come at you.
n5-kuru-rai.description: The look-alike is 米, 'rice', the piece tucked inside this kanji too. 米 turns on one central crossing point with four loose dashes flung to the corners and nothing across the top. 来 lays a flat line along its top and a short crossbar through the middle, so its centre reads like a ladder, not an X. A flat roof on top means 来; two loose dots mean 米.

n5-kyuu.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>nine</radical> radical and the <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji are the same character, so this one lands in your memory for free.
n5-kyuu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman lines up a shot with a pool <reading>cue</reading> instead of a rod. The ninth ball he sinks leaps back out of the water like a hooked fish, and he shouts <reading>きゅう</reading> at the splash.
n5-kyuu.description: Both 九 and 力 end in a hooked stroke, but the hooks point opposite ways. In 九 the final stroke sweeps wide to the right and flicks up, leaving that side open. In 力 it drops nearly straight and hooks back to the left at the foot, so the shape stays narrow. At the top, 九 has a short slant the body crosses over, while 力 opens with a bent stroke that makes a hard corner.

n5-ma-interval.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>gate</radical> with its two swinging doors thrown open. Right in the gap between them, the <radical>sun</radical> is hanging low, filling the opening with light. That sliver of sun caught in the gate is the space between things — an interval, the gap <kanji>between</kanji>.
n5-ma-interval.reading_mnemonic: A guard named Kan stands watch in that gateway, timing exactly how long the sun lingers in the gap. Every time the interval passes he shouts "<reading>かん</reading>!" and slams one door shut.
n5-ma-interval.description: 間 and 聞 are the same gate frame with different contents. 間 sets 日, the sun, inside the gateway. 聞 stands an ear there instead. What is framed by the gate settles it every time.

n5-machi.meaning_mnemonic: A farmer paces around his single square <radical>rice field</radical> every single day. Slowly other families build houses right along its edges. Soon a whole <kanji>town</kanji> surrounds that one small field.
n5-machi.reading_mnemonic: The town mayor climbs onto a soapbox in the square and announces he's the big chief now: "I'm in charge — call me <reading>ちょう</reading>!" Every time you walk into this town, you hear that same booming ちょう echoing off the buildings.
n5-machi.description: Means "town" and shows up in place names and words for local districts and neighborhoods.

n5-mae.meaning_mnemonic: A cow lowers its <radical>horns</radical> to the <radical>ground</radical> to guard the <radical>knife</radical> it dropped, so anyone crossing the yard by <radical>moon</radical>light has to freeze right in <kanji>front</kanji> of it.
n5-mae.reading_mnemonic: Long before sunrise, a monk sweeps the gravel yard out front and bows to the last of the moon. The other monks call him <reading>Zen</reading> because, whatever the hour, he is already there, and he answers to <reading>ぜん</reading> without looking up.

n5-mai-every.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>chevron</radical> on the sign with <radical>do not</radical> underneath it turns up at <kanji>every</kanji> single corner in town.
n5-mai-every.reading_mnemonic: The clock belongs to Mai, who winds it every morning and shouts "My time!" as it rings. Hear her name <reading>まい</reading> as the sound that hammers home the routine — every day, まい, まい, まい.
n5-mai-every.description: Means "every" and shows up in common time words for recurring events, such as every day, every week, and every morning.

n5-man.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>ten thousand</radical> radical and the <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> kanji are the same, so this is one review you get for nothing.
n5-man.reading_mnemonic: Koichi is restocking the onigiri shelf when a deliveryman named <reading>Manny</reading> wheels in ten thousand identical rice balls on one groaning trolley. Asked how many more are out in the truck, Manny sighs <reading>まん</reading>, counts the pile twice, loses the number both times, and gives up.
n5-man.description: The look-alike 方 (direction / person) puts a short slanted stroke above its first horizontal line; 'ten thousand' has no stroke there. Its last stroke also drops in a near-straight squarish leg, where 'ten thousand' swings that stroke out in one wide sweep.

n5-me-eye.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new to memorise here, because the <kanji>eye</kanji> kanji is simply the <radical>eye</radical> radical you have already seen, identical in shape and meaning.
n5-me-eye.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a birdwatcher presses both eyes to her binoculars for a solid hour, until campfire <reading>smoke</reading> drifts across her lenses and all she can splutter is <reading>もく</reading>. She rubs her streaming eyes and misses the owl completely.
n5-me-eye.description: The look-alikes are 日 (day or sun) and 自 (self). 目 has three lines inside its upright box, splitting it into four stacked compartments. 日 has only one line across the middle, leaving just two. 自 is the same box as 目 but with a short slanted stroke added on top, like a finger pointing at your own nose.

n5-meiname.meaning_mnemonic: In the <radical>evening</radical> nobody can see your face, so your <radical>mouth</radical> has to give your <kanji>name</kanji>.
n5-meiname.reading_mnemonic: A performer named Mei struts into Koichi's konbini and belts out "<reading>めい</reading>, that's my name, don't wear it out!" She spells it letter by letter until the whole shop knows exactly who she is.
n5-meiname.description: 名 and 多 both start with the same slanted three-stroke piece. 名 finishes with a small closed box beneath it. 多 repeats that slanted piece a second time instead, so it is one shape stacked twice.

n5-michi.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>road</radical> narrow enough to feel like the <radical>neck</radical> of a bottle is still the only <kanji>way</kanji> through.
n5-michi.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the road you meet a doe standing in the middle of the path, blocking the way. She won't budge, so you call out "<reading>どう</reading> do I get past you?" — and the doe just chews and stares, owning the whole road.
n5-michi.description: Means road or way; a very common kanji seen in words for streets, paths, and figurative "ways" of doing things.

n5-migi.meaning_mnemonic: Once your <radical>left hand</radical> is busy holding the bowl, the only hand free to lift food to your <radical>mouth</radical> is your <kanji>right</kanji>.
n5-migi.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Woo</reading> eats his lunch at the riverbank one-handed, his left hand still gripping the oar, and his clumsy right keeps dropping rice down his shirt until he lets out a long <reading>う</reading>. Every lost mouthful earns another flat <reading>う</reading>.
n5-migi.description: The look-alikes are 左 (left) and 石 (stone). All three place a shape beneath a hand-like top. In 右 that top is a short slant crossing a short flat stroke, with 口 right under it. 左 keeps the same top. Its lower part is a narrow shape with a flat foot, not a closed box. 石 keeps the 口 underneath. Its top stroke stretches into one long flat overhang with a square corner, like a cliff.

n5-mimi.meaning_mnemonic: Good news for once, the <radical>ear</radical> radical you already know and the <kanji>ear</kanji> kanji are the very same character.
n5-mimi.reading_mnemonic: A cat curls up inside the one enormous bell at Grandma Kane's shrine just as a visitor swings the rope. It rockets out past your ear going <reading>じ</reading>, and all you manage is a weak <reading>gee</reading>. Every cat on the mossy steps now watches that rope instead of sleeping.

n5-minami.meaning_mnemonic: Two <radical>horns</radical> poke out of a <radical>wide box</radical> lashed to the only wall that stays <radical>dry</radical> and warm through <radical>ten</radical> winters, and a wall like that faces <kanji>south</kanji>.
n5-minami.reading_mnemonic: Nan sets her deck chair against the south wall of the barn each morning, beside the old crate with the horns poking out. Ask why she never sits on the shady north side and she grumbles that it gets <reading>なん</reading> of the afternoon sun, dragging the word out as she tips her hat down. Everyone just calls her <reading>Nan</reading>.

n5-miru.meaning_mnemonic: Take an <radical>eye</radical> (目) and stand it up on a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> (儿), and suddenly it can <radical>see</radical> and walk around anywhere it wants. Where does an eye on legs go? Out into the world, to look at everything. So this is what it means to <kanji>see</kanji>.
n5-miru.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, drags you over to his wall of antique swords because he wants you to see his newest one. "<reading>けん</reading>! けん!" he barks, pawing at the blade until you finally look.
n5-miru.description: Means "see" and is the base of the common verb 見る (to see/look); it shows up constantly in everyday words about looking and watching.

n5-moku.meaning_mnemonic: Here the <radical>tree</radical> radical and the <kanji>tree</kanji> kanji line up stroke for stroke, trunk, spreading branch, and roots gripping the soil.
n5-moku.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles inside her old oak whenever the wind blows, until a hiker carves his initials into her bark. She leans out of the trunk to <reading>mock</reading> him, repeating every word he says in a flat little voice. He drops the knife and runs, her <reading>もく</reading> chasing him down the trail.
n5-moku.description: The look-alike 本 (book / origin) is this same tree with one extra short bar across the foot of the trunk, just above where the roots split. 木 leaves that space clean. A low bar on the trunk means 本, not 木.

n5-nagai.meaning_mnemonic: Hair falling well past the shoulders with one stroke trailing off the bottom of it is unmistakably <kanji>long</kanji>.
n5-nagai.reading_mnemonic: That long-bearded elder is the leader of a whole troupe of butterflies, and he lets one land on his flowing hair — a <reading>ちょう</reading> (butterfly). Every time you see this kanji, picture the ちょう resting on the leader's long locks.
n5-nagai.description: Means long or leader; shows up in words for length, seniority, and being the head of something, like a school principal or a company chief.

n5-naka.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> shoved straight down through a wide <radical>mouth</radical> stops dead at the exact <kanji>middle</kanji>, pinning everything trapped in there.
n5-naka.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, will not budge from the dead center of that speared mouth, and each time you try to lift him off he just squeaks <reading>ちゅう</reading> and grips the stick harder. He would <reading>chew</reading> straight through it before he let anyone take his spot in the middle.

n5-nana.meaning_mnemonic: Every hour you spent learning the radical <radical>seven</radical> is paid back here, because the <kanji>seven</kanji> kanji is the exact same character.
n5-nana.reading_mnemonic: Seven of Grandma Kane's shrine cats line up on the mossy steps at supper. Grandma is certain the sly black one <reading>cheats</reading>, slipping back for seconds the moment she looks away, so she counts them aloud and the sneak always lands on <reading>しち</reading>. Seven cats, and <reading>しち</reading> is the guilty one.
n5-nana.description: The look-alike is 十 (ten). In 十 the crossing stroke is a straight vertical down through the center, ending pointing straight down in a clean plus. In 七 that stroke crosses higher, then bends hard right along the bottom and flicks up, so the shape leans and hooks.

n5-nen.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>year</kanji> that passes, you scratch one more <radical>chevron</radical> into the sun-<radical>dry</radical> shield-board you keep staked in the <radical>ground</radical> beside the gate.
n5-nen.reading_mnemonic: By the gate at Grandma Kane's shrine stands that scratched tally board, and a fat cat called <reading>Nan</reading> sharpens her claws on it every day. Each New Year, Grandma adds a fresh notch, the cat complains about the dulled edge, and her long flat meow drags out as <reading>ねん</reading>.

n5-ni.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>two</radical> radical walked straight into the kanji list without changing a stroke, so the <kanji>two</kanji> kanji costs you nothing new.
n5-ni.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a sprinter called <reading>Knee</reading> clips the second hurdle and comes down hard on both knees. He stays in the grass hissing <reading>に</reading> through his teeth, one hiss for each knee. Second hurdle, two knees, one sound.

n5-nichi.meaning_mnemonic: Because the <radical>sun</radical> radical and the <kanji>day</kanji> kanji are the very same character, every hour you spent learning radicals is quietly paying you back here.
n5-nichi.reading_mnemonic: Every day a mountain-trail ranger called <reading>Neech</reading> climbs up to check the lone vending machine, and every day the sun has already cooked every can inside into warm soup. He kicks the machine once, mutters <reading>にち</reading>, and writes off another wasted day.
n5-nichi.description: The look-alike 白 (white) is this same barred box with one extra short stroke flicked onto the top; take that flick away and you are back to 'day'. The look-alike 目 (eye) is a taller box with two bars across the middle instead of one, stacking three sections where 'day' has only two.

n5-nichiyou.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>pheasant</radical> that only calls when the <radical>sun</radical> is properly up marks off another <kanji>weekday</kanji>.
n5-nichiyou.reading_mnemonic: Yoko, exhausted, groans "no more, no more" as she crosses off day after day on the wall calendar. Every square she reaches she moans <reading>よう</reading>, よう, because to her every single weekday feels the same.

n5-nishi.meaning_mnemonic: No new work here, because the <radical>west</radical> radical, that sun climbing down into its crate for the night, is the <kanji>west</kanji> kanji with not one stroke moved.
n5-nishi.reading_mnemonic: At the school, when the teacher asks which way the sun goes down, Sei's hand is up before anyone has even finished hearing the question. Too pleased with himself to wait his turn, he leans back and says <reading>せい</reading>. It is the right answer, because that is the sound you <reading>say</reading> for west.
n5-nishi.description: The look-alike is 四, meaning four. West has a separate horizontal lid across the very top that pokes out past the sides, and the two upright strokes inside rise up to meet it. Four is a plain sealed rectangle with a flat top and no overhang, and its two inner strokes curl apart at the bottom without touching the top.

n5-nomu.meaning_mnemonic: On the left sits food and eating. On the right, a person opens their mouth wide in a <radical>yawn</radical>. But this mouth isn't tired — it's tipping a glass back, gulping something down. Food beside that gaping, thirsty mouth: that's <kanji>drink</kanji>.
n5-nomu.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a regular named Inn slaps a cold can on the beeping till and says the same thing every single day: "First, I drink!" You can hear the 「<reading>いん</reading>」 right at the front of Inn's name as he cracks it open.
n5-nomu.description: Means "drink"; the everyday kanji in the verb 飲む, to drink.

n5-onna.meaning_mnemonic: You get the <kanji>woman</kanji> kanji for free today, since it is the same <radical>woman</radical> radical you already practised, shape and meaning untouched.
n5-onna.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a woman called <reading>Jo</reading> has one job, which is shooing the cats off the mossy steps. Every time she lifts one down she mutters <reading>じょ</reading> under her breath, and by evening she has said it so often that the cats have started to purr the sound back at her.

n5-ooi-ta.meaning_mnemonic: One <radical>evening</radical> stacked straight on top of another <radical>evening</radical> is how you end up with <kanji>many</kanji>.
n5-ooi-ta.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, Ta counts the coins in the improbable vending machine. There are far too many to hold. "<reading>た</reading>, た, た," she taps each one as they spill from her hands. There are just too many.
n5-ooi-ta.description: 多 is the same slanted piece written twice, one stacked below the other. 名 writes that piece once and puts a small closed box underneath it instead.

n5-otoko.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the <kanji>man</kanji>.
n5-otoko.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

n5-roku.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>number eight</radical> standing tall, and then set a little <radical>lid</radical> right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means <kanji>six</kanji>.
n5-roku.reading_mnemonic: A rock star climbs onto the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and belts out six songs to the empty air. Every time he screams "<reading>ろく</reading>!" a cat appears, until six of them are yowling backup. That rock (ろく) show is how you hear six.
n5-roku.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

n5-san.meaning_mnemonic: Copy the flat <radical>ground</radical> line, then draw it twice more above itself, and the stubby ladder of level rungs you get is <kanji>three</kanji>.
n5-san.reading_mnemonic: A shrine cat named <reading>Sun</reading> claims the third stone step at Grandma Kane's as her bed. Every visitor forced to step over her murmurs <reading>さん</reading>, half a greeting and half an apology, and by the third one she purrs for more.

n5-sei-life.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new here, the <radical>life</radical> radical and the <kanji>life</kanji> kanji are one character, and it also covers birth because birth is just where a life begins.
n5-sei-life.reading_mnemonic: In a hallway at Sei's school, the teacher barely finishes asking what that first shoot through the soil stands for. Sei's hand is already up, uniform crease-perfect, and she <reading>says</reading> <reading>せい</reading> before anyone else draws breath. She looks quietly smug about beating the whole class to it.

n5-sen.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a single <radical>slash</radical> across your tally of <radical>ten</radical> and the whole count suddenly jumps to a <kanji>thousand</kanji>.
n5-sen.reading_mnemonic: Back at that smeared tally wall in the school hallway, Sei counts the marks, gives up, and decides to just <reading>send</reading> the whole impossible number through as one lump sum. It goes as <reading>せん</reading>, a flat thousand that nobody is ever going to recount.
n5-sen.description: 千 opens with a slash from the upper right, above one horizontal and the upright. 十 (ten) is that shape without the slash. 午 (noon) keeps the slash but runs two horizontals. 干 (dry or shield) has two horizontals as well, but a flat straight top instead of a slash.

n5-sensei-saki.meaning_mnemonic: The one whose striding <radical>human legs</radical> have already worn a diagonal <radical>slash</radical> of path into the bare <radical>earth</radical> is the one out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of us.
n5-sensei-saki.reading_mnemonic: On the steep mountain trail, a hiker called <reading>Sen</reading> stays exactly one switchback in front of you the whole climb, so all you ever catch is her fresh bootprints in the mud. Shout up to ask how much farther, and the only word that drifts back down is <reading>せん</reading>.

n5-sha-car.meaning_mnemonic: An axle drawn straight through a box of cargo with a wheel at either end is a <kanji>car</kanji>.
n5-sha-car.reading_mnemonic: A show-off racer revs his engine outside Koichi's konbini and shouts "Watch me!" He peels out so fast all you hear is a screech of "<reading>しゃ</reading>!" The vehicle vanishes down the street. Every time you see this car kanji, that "しゃ!" is the last sound it makes.
n5-sha-car.description: 車 and 重 are the same boxy stack, but 重 is taller and runs an extra horizontal through the middle. Count the horizontal strokes crossing the body: 重 always has one more than 車.

n5-shi-city.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> pulled over row after row of hanging <radical>cloth</radical> is a whole <kanji>city</kanji> of stalls.
n5-shi-city.reading_mnemonic: The busiest stall belongs to Shi, a sharp-eyed vendor who greets every shopper crossing the market with a cheerful 「<reading>し</reading>!」. Follow her voice and you'll always find the center of the city.
n5-shi-city.description: Means city or market; shows up in words for towns and municipal places like 市 (city) and city names.

n5-shiro-white.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> with one extra ray coming off the top is too bright to be any colour but <kanji>white</kanji>.
n5-shiro-white.reading_mnemonic: The dazzling light spooks a startled hawk perched on the konbini roof; it beats its wings once and goes, <reading>はく</reading>, hacking out a cough as it flaps into the too-bright sky. Hear that はく every time you see this pure white flash.
n5-shiro-white.description: All four are the same box with bars inside, and the top settles it. 白 caps the box with a small flick. 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal. 自 uses a short slash instead. 日 has no cap at all.

n5-shita.meaning_mnemonic: Hang the tortoise's <radical>divination</radical> mark off the underside of the <radical>ground</radical> line and it dangles <kanji>down</kanji> into the dark where no one reads it.
n5-shita.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow gives up on the power lines and drops down under the riverbank bridge, into the dark below the road. It is damp and empty down there, so he just huffs one small flame and mutters <reading>か</reading> to himself. It comes out flat, like the tail end of the word <reading>car</reading>.

n5-shou-small.meaning_mnemonic: You get this one free, because the <radical>small</radical> radical you already know is the <kanji>small</kanji> kanji unchanged, right down to the two fingers pinching that speck.
n5-shou-small.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, sets up on the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini, the only stage that fits him. He snaps his small white gloves, a dove flops out, and he bills the whole trick as his big <reading>show</reading>. Over the beeping till he just shouts <reading>しょう</reading> again until a customer finally claps.
n5-shou-small.description: The look-alike is 少, meaning few or little. It is this kanji with one stroke added: a short slanting stroke laid over the top right, making four strokes instead of three. If the centre hook and its two side marks stand alone with nothing above them, it is small; if a stray diagonal caps the top, it is few.

n5-shu-week.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>week</kanji> is just how long it takes to <radical>advance</radical> the whole way around the <radical>circumference</radical> of the calendar and trip back over your own Monday footprints.
n5-shu-week.reading_mnemonic: Sei jogs one lap of the school field every morning for a week, and by the seventh her right shoe's sole has peeled clean off from tracing the same circle. She lifts the flapping <reading>shoe</reading> and groans <reading>しゅう</reading>, the wet slap it makes on the track. Seven laps, one dead <reading>しゅう</reading>, one week gone.

n5-sui.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>water</radical> radical and the <kanji>water</kanji> kanji are the exact same splash, one central stream with two trickles flying off, frozen mid-air.
n5-sui.reading_mnemonic: A big white swan has claimed the riverbank, and every time someone kneels to wash clothes she flaps up and drags a hard <reading>sweep</reading> of spray across their back. You stand there soaked and dripping. That cold slap of river water off her wings is the sound <reading>すい</reading>.

n5-sukunai.meaning_mnemonic: Take something <radical>small</radical> — that hook with two flanking dots — and slice one more dot away with a downward stroke. Now there's even less than small: barely anything left. When you take a bite out of small, what remains is <kanji>few</kanji>.
n5-sukunai.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, opens his white-gloved hand to reveal only a few crumbs of confetti — "<reading>しょう</reading> time!" he squeaks, and even the doves look unimpressed by how little there is. His whole act, like everything about him, is small and few.
n5-sukunai.description: 少 is 小 with one extra stroke: a slash sweeping down and to the left below the base. Take that tail away and you are back to 小.

n5-suwaru.meaning_mnemonic: Anywhere with a <radical>shelter</radical> over it is somewhere two people can <radical>sit</radical>, so that is where they <kanji>sit</kanji>.
n5-suwaru.reading_mnemonic: The person who settles onto that patch of earth is Zara, and the moment she sits she lets out a long, satisfied "<reading>ざ</reading>あ" of relief. Every time you see someone plop down here, you hear Zara's ざ.
n5-suwaru.description: Means "sit"; shows up in words about sitting down, seats, and taking a seat.

n5-taberu.meaning_mnemonic: A roof pitched over a heap of rice with two chopsticks laid across it is the sign for <kanji>eat</kanji>.
n5-taberu.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful line cook at Koichi's konbini slings hot lunches under the fluorescent lights, and every time a tray lands he shouts his catchphrase: <reading>しょく</reading>, しょく, come and get it! You hear しょく and your stomach knows it's time to eat.
n5-taberu.description: Means eat or food; shows up in everyday words for meals, eating, and food, and as the verb "to eat."

n5-takai.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> over a <radical>mouth</radical> looking out across open <radical>prairie</radical> has been built very <kanji>tall</kanji>.
n5-takai.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, is jealous of that tall tower, so he stacks his onigiri shelves higher and higher until they're the tallest — and priciest — display in town. As the tower of rice balls wobbles, he shouts <reading>こう</reading> to warn a customer before it topples.

n5-tatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person planted firmly on the ground, feet apart, refusing to budge — they <radical>stand</radical> there, solid and upright. That single image, a person rooted on the earth, is the whole character: to <kanji>stand</kanji>.
n5-tatsu.reading_mnemonic: A soldier named Ritsu snaps to attention on the mountain trail, standing so straight you could measure a wall against him. Every time someone shouts "<reading>りつ</reading>!" he stands up even taller.
n5-tatsu.description: Means "stand"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words about standing up, standing something upright, and establishing or setting things in place.

n5-te-hand.meaning_mnemonic: This one is free if you learned your radicals well, because the <radical>hand</radical> radical and the <kanji>hand</kanji> kanji are one and the same character.
n5-te-hand.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon strolls into Koichi's konbini and settles on the onigiri shelf by the door. Koichi waves one flat hand at it, hissing <reading>しゅ</reading>, <reading>shoo</reading>, while the till keeps beeping. It takes both hands and a broom before the bird finally leaves.

n5-ten.meaning_mnemonic: One flat <radical>ground</radical> line laid above the arms of the <radical>big</radical> outstretched person turns everything higher than it into <kanji>heaven</kanji>.
n5-ten.reading_mnemonic: Out on the school sports field, the gym teacher the kids call <reading>Ten</reading> makes the whole class lie flat on the ground. Arms flung out wide, faces up at the open sky, nobody moves. He walks the rows counting slowly, and the drill ends when he reaches <reading>てん</reading>.
n5-ten.description: The one to watch is 大, meaning big. 天 has two horizontal strokes stacked at the top, while 大 has just the single crossbar for the arms. That short top line is the whole difference.

n5-tomeru.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Divination</radical> cracks that all run into one footprint are telling you exactly where to <kanji>stop</kanji>.
n5-tomeru.reading_mnemonic: Right where you stopped, you hear a sharp "<reading>し</reading>!" — someone shushing you. It's the vending machine at the top of the trail, hissing "し, し" as it refuses to dispense until you stop and wait. That shushing し is the sound to hold onto.
n5-tomeru.description: Means "stop" and is the base of common verbs like 止まる and 止める, showing up anywhere something halts or is brought to a halt.

n5-uenagashi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, the tortoise's <radical>divination</radical> crack rises from the flat <radical>ground</radical> line with everything it has to say pointing <kanji>up</kanji>.
n5-uenagashi.reading_mnemonic: Joe the window washer hangs in his cradle above the shrine roof, polishing the top of the great bell. When Grandma Kane calls to ask where he is, the only answer that floats down is <reading>じょう</reading>, the one direction he ever points. He says it like the name <reading>Joe</reading>, stretched long.

n5-uru-baku.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>samurai</radical> with a <radical>cover</radical> over his crest and his <radical>human legs</radical> behind a stall has come to <kanji>sell</kanji>.
n5-uru-baku.reading_mnemonic: The vendor keeps yelling one thing at every customer who walks past: "Buy! <reading>ばい</reading>, ばい, one for you and one for the baby!" He'll sell to anyone who slows down, and every pitch ends on that same ばい.

n5-ushiro.meaning_mnemonic: Each <radical>step</radical> you take drags a <radical>trailing foot</radical> caught on a <radical>tiny thread</radical>, so that foot always lands a beat <kanji>behind</kanji> the rest of you.
n5-ushiro.reading_mnemonic: At the school sports field, a gopher lines up for the relay with a thread off his own shoe wound round his back foot. The starter yells <reading>ご</reading> to make the runners <reading>go</reading>, and the gopher spends the entire lap one step behind, picking at the knot.

n5-yama.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a freebie, since the <radical>mountain</radical> radical and the <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji are the exact same character.
n5-yama.reading_mnemonic: A hiker slogs up the steep mountain trail toward the lone vending machine at the top. Right as she reaches the summit the <reading>sun</reading> clears the ridge and blinds her, and all she can manage is <reading>さん</reading> before feeding in her coins.

n5-yasui.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>woman</radical> kneeling gracefully inside a snug little house, the <radical>roof</radical> pulled down over her like a blanket. Nothing can reach her in here — she is safe, the rent is nothing, everything is calm. A woman tucked safely under a roof is cheap and <kanji>peaceful</kanji>.
n5-yasui.reading_mnemonic: She's spreading sweet red <reading>あん</reading> (bean paste) on a bun, humming, utterly at peace. Every bite is cheap comfort — say あん and taste that calm.
n5-yasui.description: 安 means cheap or peaceful, and shows up in words for low prices, safety, and being at ease.

n5-yasumu.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, you spot a <radical>person</radical> slumped sideways against a <radical>tree</radical>, leaning into the trunk like it's the comfiest chair in the world. A <radical>person</radical> plus the tree they're propped against — that's someone taking a well-earned <kanji>rest</kanji>.
n5-yasumu.reading_mnemonic: The hiker leaning on that tree lets out a huge, happy sigh — "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" — the sound of every muscle finally letting go. Every time you picture that person melting into rest, you hear that きゅう escape.
n5-yasumu.description: Means "rest" and shows up in everyday words for taking breaks and days off, like 休み.

n5-yon.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside a doorless <radical>enclosure</radical>, your <radical>human legs</radical> pace off all <kanji>four</kanji> of its walls before you admit there is no way out.
n5-yon.reading_mnemonic: A sheep called <reading>She</reading> is stuck in the same doorless enclosure you paced earlier, tramping its four walls on a loop. At each corner she halts and bleats <reading>し</reading> at the blank stone, waiting for a door to appear. Four corners, four bleats, still no way out.
n5-yon.description: The look-alike is 西 west. In 四 the mark inside the box is a small pair of splayed legs that hang from the top and spread downward without touching the walls. 西 is noticeably taller, and its two inner strokes stand straight up like poles fixed to the top edge.
